items.title: 68003_Eddie Sauter oral history interview
items.q: I heard an album that Johnny Mandel wrote

ctx.x: It gets a very special sound right away, because I tried doubling it with accordion or organ too when I get little ones like that. Accordion is a little less objectionable than flute and yet it takes the edge off the fiddle is what it does.

I heard an album that Johnny Mandel wrote about twenty years ago for David Allyn and I was with David Allyn when I heard it, and he was saying, do you hear the organ? Apparently Johnny used organ in the same way you mentioned, to bolster the strings and it was so subtly done that I really had to strain to catch it at all.

It all depends what the engineer does. I latched onto that doing Broadway shows, because they never have enough strings. The trick is to always have them play under, never to play over but then when the engineer comes on, he puts them right up even, and the guys don't always watch it either, because they can't hear; they're always put in a place where they can't hear.

items.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I think I met him once through Manny Albam but I was shy you know

ctx.x: I did, I interviewed him for this program 15 years ago.
I think I met him once through Manny Albam but I was shy you know, and it was just in passing, I never really got to sit down and talk to Eddie.
You two would have enjoyed that, you know, you were kindred spirits.
